Newly hatched juveniles of the Northern spring amphipod emerge from the maternal brood pouch at a remarkably small size, with a total length at birth of 0.19 centimeters [Lb = 0.19 centimeters]. This initial body dimension is consistent with the modest neonatal sizes documented across the Gammaridae, reflecting the substantial number of offspring brooded per clutch. Shortly after emergence, these neonates begin exogenous feeding and commence a period of rapid somatic growth. Field surveys in first-order streams of the Great Lakes region have provided extensive morphometric data for this species. Among the most frequently reported metrics is the total length at puberty, measured at 0.7 centimeters [Lp = 0.7 centimeters], which marks the onset of functional reproductive capability. Individuals attaining this length typically exhibit developing secondary sexual characteristics such as enlarged gnathopods in males and elongated brood plates in females, though the precise timing of this transition varies with local thermal regimes.

The life history of Gammarus pseudolimnaeus is notably temperature-dependent, influencing both developmental rates and asymptotic body size. At a water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], field-caught adults reach an ultimate total length of 1.6 centimeters [Li = 1.6 centimeters], a value derived from the largest specimens collected during autumnal population surveys. This maximum dimension is comparable to that reported for other cool-adapted gammarids in the Laurentian mixed forest ecoregion. Under these same thermal conditions, the maximum recorded lifespan extends to 460 days [am = 460 days] for individuals held in stream-side mesocosms that approximated natural flow regimes and leaf-litter inputs at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This longevity figure integrates mortality from both senescent processes and seasonal predation pressure, particularly from drift-feeding salmonids. The relatively extended lifespan relative to body size reflects the low metabolic demands of the cold-water habitat and the species' ability to exploit allochthonous detrital resources throughout the year.

Data on mass at key life stages have been gathered from laboratory-reared cohorts maintained on conditioned leaf discs. The dry weight at birth in this species is 0.00002 grams , reflecting the minimal investment of maternal resources into each individual offspring. As juveniles progress through successive instars, they accumulate somatic tissue and eventually attain a dry weight at puberty of 0.00153 grams . This represents a nearly two-order-of-magnitude increase in biomass from the neonatal stage and corresponds closely with the developmental milestone marked by the 0.7 centimeter total length. The ultimate dry weight for fully grown adults has been recorded at 0.0115 grams , a figure derived from ovigerous females that had completed their terminal molt. These mass-based measurements underscore the species' relatively modest body plan and its reliance on efficient nutrient assimilation from decaying organic matter.

Reproductive output in this amphipod has been quantified through intensive field sampling of the Driftless Area streams. The maximum daily reproduction rate, averaged from field data collected at a water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], reflects a combination of brood size and interbrood interval. Females produce clutches containing, on average, 15 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 15 eggs per brood], with a maximum recorded clutch frequency of approximately 1.5 broods per month [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 broods per month] during the peak reproductive season. This yields an annual reproductive output of roughly 135 offspring per female [Ri = annual reproductive output of roughly 135 offspring per female], a rate that positions Gammarus pseudolimnaeus as a moderately iteroparous crustacean compared to other members of the genus. Ovigerous females were collected from March through October, with peak egg-bearing incidence observed in late spring. The reproductive pattern appears to be linked to the availability of high-quality microbial biofilms on decomposing leaves, which provide essential lipids for vitellogenesis.

Developmental milestones have been investigated under controlled temperature regimes to isolate thermal effects on ontogeny. At an incubation temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], embryonic development within the brood pouch culminates in the release of fully formed juveniles at 25 days [ab = 25 days], a duration approximately one week shorter than that observed at 8 °C. The age at sexual maturation, or puberty, is expressed as the time since birth at puberty and has been estimated at 130 days [tp = 130 days] for individuals reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This value, originally approximated from data on the congener Gammarus pulex, appears consistent with the growth rates and molt frequencies recorded in pseudolimnaeus under similar thermal conditions. The relatively rapid attainment of reproductive competence at warmer temperatures likely confers a selective advantage in intermittent stream habitats where growing seasons are compressed. Continued research into the thermal reaction norms of this species remains essential for predicting population responses to climate-driven shifts in stream temperatures.
